The CRUD operations from Post 01 take a filter as the first argument. The filter is where MongoDB's query expressiveness lives — comparison, logical, element-existence, array, regex, full-text, and geospatial operators all compose into one JSON-like predicate. This post covers every operator family, projection extras ($elemMatch, $slice, $), the right sort/limit/skip discipline, and the range pagination pattern that scales to millions of rows where .skip() collapses.
Series map: 00 Foundations → 01 CRUD → 02 Query Operators (this post) → 03 Indexes → 04 Query Optimization → 05 Aggregation Basics → … → 17 Drivers & Case Studies.

Use every comparison operator: $eq, $ne, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $in, $nin.
Combine with logical operators: $and, $or, $nor, $not.
Use element operators: $exists, $type.
Match arrays correctly: $all, $elemMatch, $size.
Use $regex, $text, and $expr for advanced predicates.
Use projection extras: $elemMatch, $slice, the positional $.
Paginate with range queries instead of .skip() at scale.

Operator · Meaning
$eq · equals
$ne · not equals
$gt / $gte · greater than / or equal
$lt / $lte · less than / or equal
$in · value in array of options
$nin · value NOT in array
db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 25, $lte: 40 } }) // 25 < age ≤ 40
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ["book", "pen"] } })
db.users.find({ status: { $nin: ["banned", "deleted"] } })
Bare equality is the most common form:
db.users.find({ name: "Ada" }) // same as { name: { $eq: "Ada" } }

db.users.find({ tags: "math" }) // matches if "math" is an element of tags
db.users.find({ tags: ["math", "eng"] }) // matches if tags EQUALS exactly ["math","eng"]
Subtle and important. The first form is "contains"; the second is "exactly equals this array". Use $all (Chapter 4) for "contains all of".

db.users.find({ email: { $exists: true } }) // field present (any value, even null)
db.users.find({ email: { $exists: false } }) // field absent
db.users.find({ deleted_at: { $exists: false } }) // not soft-deleted

db.users.find({ age: { $type: "number" } })
db.users.find({ tags: { $type: "array" } })
db.users.find({ joined: { $type: "date" } })
db.misc.find({ x: { $type: ["int", "long", "double"] } }) // multiple types
Useful in legacy / dirty collections where a field might be a string in some docs, number in others.

db.users.find({ tags: { $all: ["math", "eng"] } })
// matches docs where tags has both "math" AND "eng" (any order, may have more)

db.users.find({ tags: { $size: 3 } })
No $lt/$gt variants on $size. For "more than N elements" use an indexed counter field (tag_count) updated alongside writes.

db.users.find({ email: /@example\.com$/ })
db.users.find({ name: { $regex: "^Ad", $options: "i" } }) // case-insensitive prefix
$options flag · Meaning
i · case-insensitive
m · multiline ^ / $
s · . matches newlines
x · ignore whitespace + allow # comments in pattern

A left-anchored regex (/^Ad/) can use a B-tree index on the field. Anything else does a scan within the index range or a full collection scan.
db.users.find({ name: /^Ad/ }) // index-friendly
db.users.find({ name: /Ada$/ }) // not index-friendly
db.users.find({ name: /Ada/ }) // not index-friendly (no left anchor)
db.users.find({ name: /^Ada/i }) // index-friendly only if collation matches
For substring + fuzzy + multi-language matching, prefer text indexes (next) or Atlas Search (Post 16).

A text index enables $text queries:
db.articles.createIndex({ title: "text", body: "text" })
db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "mongodb tutorial" } })
db.articles.find({ $text: { $search: "\"exact phrase\" -excluded" } })
db.articles.find(
{ $text: { $search: "mongodb" } },
{ score: { $meta: "textScore" } }
).sort({ score: { $meta: "textScore" } })
Limits:
One text index per collection.
No phrase scoring nuance, no language-aware stemming beyond a basic set.
No autocomplete / fuzzy out of the box.
For serious search → Atlas Search (Lucene-based, faceted, autocomplete, fuzzy, multi-language) — Post 16.

db.users.find({}, { name: 1, email: 1, _id: 0 }) // include name+email, drop _id
db.users.find({}, { password: 0 }) // exclude only password
You can't mix include + exclude except for _id.

db.users.find({}, { tags: { $slice: 5 } }) // first 5
db.users.find({}, { tags: { $slice: -3 } }) // last 3
db.users.find({}, { tags: { $slice: [10, 5] } }) // skip 10, take 5

db.orders.find({ status: "paid" })
.sort({ at: -1 })
.limit(20)
.skip(40)
For small offsets this is fine. Cost of .skip(N): server scans N + limit documents in sort order, then discards the N. For N = 10,000 on a million-row collection that's painful even with an index.

db.orders.find({ user_id: 1 }).hint({ user_id: 1, at: -1 }) // force this index
db.orders.find({ user_id: 1 }).comment("dashboard-recent-orders") // tag for profiler
db.orders.find({ user_id: 1 }).maxTimeMS(500) // abort if > 500 ms
comment surfaces in db.currentOp() + the slow-query profiler — invaluable for tracking which app code issued a given query in production.
maxTimeMS is a safety net against runaway queries. Always set it in user-facing paths.

db.users.distinct("country") // [ "UK", "US", "JP" ]
db.users.distinct("country", { age: { $gte: 30 } })
db.users.countDocuments({ active: true }) // accurate
db.users.estimatedDocumentCount() // fast, metadata only
distinct returns an array (max 16 MB BSON). For huge distinct sets, use the aggregation $group (Post 05).

Symptom · Cause · Fix
find({ tags: ["a"] }) returns nothing · exact-array match · use tags: "a" (contains) or $all: ["a"]
find slow on large collection · no index · Post 03
Multi-condition array filter matches wrong docs · conditions applied independently · use $elemMatch
Regex full-scan · not left-anchored · anchor /^…/ or use text/Atlas Search
.skip(50000) painfully slow · offset cost · range pagination
$or slow despite indexes · each branch needs its own index · create one index per branch
find returns sub-document with full fields · no projection · always project for big docs
App appears to ignore some results · iterating cursor twice · re-issue query or .toArray() once

Using the shop dataset, write find queries for:
a) Users aged 30-40 inclusive.
b) Products costing under USD 10 OR over USD 50.
c) Orders for users 1 or 2, status "paid".
d) Users where the address field doesn't exist.
Solutions
db.users.find({ age: { $gte: 30, $lte: 40 } })
db.products.find({ $or: [{ price: { $lt: 10 } }, { price: { $gt: 50 } }] })
db.orders.find({ user_id: { $in: [1, 2] }, status: "paid" })
db.users.find({ address: { $exists: false } })
Insert sample students from Chapter 4. Write the query for "students with math grade ≥ 70" both the WRONG and RIGHT way. Confirm they return different results.
Implement a function getPage(beforeAt, limit) for orders that returns limit paid orders strictly older than beforeAt, sorted desc by at. Test with a Node script paging through 1000 synthetic orders.

find all users, returning only name, email, and the first 2 elements of tags. No _id.
Solution
db.users.find({}, { _id: 0, name: 1, email: 1, tags: { $slice: 2 } })
On a 100k-document collection (synthesise), measure find({ name: /^Ad/ }) vs find({ name: /Ad/ }) execution time. Confirm only the first uses the index efficiently (preview of Post 04 explain).
Build a text index over articles.title + body. Query "mongodb tutorial". Sort by text score.
